description: Proyecto individual enfocado en desarrollar una solución técnica basada en datos abiertos de la NASA, combinando análisis de datos, estadística y desarrollo de software/prototipado. Equipo completo (1 integrante) participando desde la sede de Concepción.
summary: Autonomous Health Monitor is a prototype that lets astronauts on long missions check their own health without waiting for Earth. Each day it records six indicators: resting heart rate, heart rate variability, sleep, mood, stress and exercise. Instead of fixed population thresholds, it compares each value with the astronaut's own baseline, the median of the previous 21 days. The result is an explainable traffic light: green, yellow or red, showing which indicators triggered the alert and a recommended action protocol. It runs fully offline. We tested the detector on 300 simulated missions per duration (60 to 180 days): it found all sleep and cardiovascular episodes, 97 to 100% of mood episodes, with 1 to 1.5% false red alarms. All data are simulated; normal values are based on NASA-funded studies of ISS crews. The code was written with an AI assistant (Claude) and is disclosed in the project.
details:
What it does: the astronaut logs six daily indicators (resting heart rate, heart rate variability, sleep, mood, stress, exercise minutes). After 10 days of calibration, each value is compared with the median of the astronaut's previous 21 days, counting only the worrying direction. Yellow means one indicator moved away from its baseline: verify and watch. Red means two or more indicators are altered on the same day, or one is altered two days in a row: act. Every alert names its causes and shows a recommended action protocol (cardiovascular, sleep and psychological state, or physical activity).

Why it matters: on a Mars mission a message to Earth can take about 20 minutes each way, so the crew must detect changes in themselves. A personal baseline adapts to each astronaut instead of using population averages, and the explanation avoids a black box.

How we built it: Python, pandas and NumPy for the detector; Streamlit and Plotly for the interface. It runs locally with no internet connection. A simulator generates missions with hidden, labelled episodes (sleep deprivation, cardiovascular alert, mood decline) so detection can be measured.

Validation: 300 simulated missions for each duration of 60, 90, 120 and 180 days. Sleep and cardiovascular episodes were detected in 100% of missions and mood decline in 97 to 100%, with 1 to 1.5% false red alarms on normal days.

Limitations: all data are simulated, not real flight data. Thresholds are statistical, not clinical; the system flags changes, it does not diagnose. Action protocols have not been reviewed by medical staff. Only sleep and exercise base values come from astronaut studies; the others are our assumptions.

Use of AI: the solution approach, the code, the demo video and its music, and these texts were produced with Claude (Anthropic) following the team member's requirements and decisions. Details are in the README.
